guides.title: How to build pressure the right way: complaints, city leaders, and press — in order
guides.summary: The accountability sequence that actually moves a landlord: document first, get advice, file real complaints, put city leaders on notice, then go public. Each step feeds the next.

steps.title: Document everything before you say anything
steps.body: Every step after this one leans on dated, verifiable records — the notice, the repair request, the inspection report. Timeline, journal, and your document vault are the foundation; pressure built on memory gets waved off.

steps.title: Get advice before filing
steps.body: Talk to legal aid or a tenant hotline first. They'll tell you which complaints fit your facts, which deadlines apply, and whether your situation has a presumption window open right now.

steps.title: File the real complaints
steps.body: File with the agencies that actually have jurisdiction — attorney general, housing/code enforcement, HUD if discrimination is in play, the licensing board if the landlord or broker is licensed. Each filing creates an official record and an investigation the landlord has to answer to.

steps.title: Put city leaders on notice
steps.body: Send a factual letter to your council member, the mayor, or your county commissioner. Not a rant — what you documented, who you filed with, and what you're asking their office to do. City leaders can route inspections and put the landlord on notice that a record exists.

steps.title: Go public only when the record can carry it
steps.body: A press release or media kit works when the facts speak for themselves. Stick to what you can document — a truthful press release is pressure a landlord can't make go away; an exaggerated one gets set aside.

steps.title: Follow up on a schedule
steps.body: Agencies and offices respond to documented persistence. Log every contact, note every deadline they give you, and follow up when it passes. The record of follow-ups itself becomes part of the pressure.

tips: Filing with multiple agencies at once is legitimate — each has different leverage.
Everything you send to a leader or reporter should be something you'd be comfortable seeing in a courtroom. Facts only.
This is accountability, not revenge — the record does the talking. If a step would only embarrass someone rather than create a record or an obligation, skip it.
guides.source: research — system procedure, not first-hand experience; review before publishing

guides.title: Mark the bill draft: comment, question, or suggest an edit
guides.summary: How to leave a comment, ask a question, or suggest an edit on the Rent Assurance & Deposit Protection Act draft at semptify.org/bill. What you send stays private until a person reads it onto the public margin.

steps.title: Open the Inkwell
steps.body: Go to semptify.org/bill and open the page called the Inkwell. If you are reading a specific clause, use the mark link on that clause's page — it opens the same form with the clause already picked.

steps.title: Pick the clause and the kind
steps.body: Choose the clause your mark is about, or leave it on general, no clause. Then pick a kind: Comment, Question, or Proposed edit.

steps.title: Write it plainly
steps.body: Say what you mean in your own words — a suggestion, a concern, a correction, or a question all count. The writing box is required. Everything else on the form is optional.

steps.title: Decide what to sign
steps.body: You can add proposed wording, your name, and a way to reach you. Your name appears publicly only if a steward reads your mark onto the margin. Your contact information is never shown.

steps.title: Send it and save the receipt code
steps.body: Submit the form. The page gives you a receipt code — write it down. It is the only way to check on your mark later.

tips: Nothing posts right away. Your mark goes into a private intake pile. A person — called a steward — reads it and decides whether it goes on the public margin with an M-number.
Leave the name field blank to stay unsigned. The contact field is never published — it is only so the steward can reach you.
The box labeled website is a trap for bots. Leave it empty.
If this is about your own housing right now — a notice, a repair, a lockout — call HOME Line at 612-728-5767 first. The mark form says so too. A proposed law cannot fix an emergency.
guides.source: verified against the live bill platform (semptify.org/bill) on 2026-11-22; drafted per handoffs/library-guide-outline.md

guides.title: Answer a mark that is already on the margin
guides.summary: How to reply to a mark someone already made on the bill draft at semptify.org/bill. Your answer links back to their mark once it is read in.

steps.title: Open the margin
steps.body: Go to semptify.org/bill and open the margin. It is the public ledger of every mark that has been read in — numbered M-0001 and up.

steps.title: Find the mark you want to answer
steps.body: Read down the list, or follow a link to a specific M-number. Each mark shows its number, its date, and the clause it is about.

steps.title: Choose 'answer by reference'
steps.body: On the mark, click or tap 'answer by reference.' It opens the Inkwell form already linked to that mark.

steps.title: Write your answer
steps.body: Say what you would add, correct, or answer. Keep it on the point you are replying to.

steps.title: Send it and save the receipt code
steps.body: Submit, then write down the receipt code. Once a steward reads your answer in, it shows on the margin as a reply to that M-number.

tips: Answers are marks too — they go through the same private intake before they show publicly.
Answer the mark, not the person. The margin is a public record, and plain and factual reads best.
guides.source: verified against the live bill platform (semptify.org/bill) on 2026-11-22; drafted per handoffs/library-guide-outline.md

guides.title: Ask for a briefing, an amendment, a position, or an answer
guides.summary: How to use the requests desk at semptify.org/bill when you need more than a comment — a briefing, a change to the draft, an organization's position, or a technical answer. You can watch your request move through its stages.

steps.title: Open the requests desk
steps.body: Go to semptify.org/bill and open Requests. The form for a new request is on that page.

steps.title: Pick what you are asking for
steps.body: Choose a request type: Briefing / fiscal walkthrough, Statutory amendment, Organization position, Technical question, or Other.

steps.title: Say it in one line
steps.body: The summary box is required — one line that says what you are asking. You can also pick the clause it relates to and add details underneath.

steps.title: Say who is asking — optional
steps.body: There is a field for your organization or role, and a contact field. The contact is for the steward only. It never shows on the public page.

steps.title: Send it and save the receipt code
steps.body: Submit the form and write down the receipt code. It is the only way to check on your request later.

tips: A request is for something that needs an answer or an action. If you only want to comment on the wording of a clause, use the Inkwell instead.
Your request moves through stages: new, reviewing, scheduled, then incorporated or declined. Check it anytime with your receipt code on the Track page.
Notes the steward leaves on your request are public. Read your request's row to see them.
guides.source: verified against the live bill platform (semptify.org/bill) on 2026-11-22; drafted per handoffs/library-guide-outline.md

guides.title: Sign the bill
guides.summary: How to add your name to the public book of supporters for the Rent Assurance & Deposit Protection Act draft at semptify.org/bill. Signing is a public act — your name publishes only because you choose it.

steps.title: Open the sign page
steps.body: Go to semptify.org/bill and open Sign the bill.

steps.title: Write your name as it should appear
steps.body: The name field is required. Whatever you write is what would publish — for example, A. Renter, St. Paul.

steps.title: Add what you want on the record — optional
steps.body: You can add your organization or town, and one line for the record. Both publish with your name.

steps.title: Add your email only if you want follow-up — optional
steps.body: The email field is never published. It exists so someone can reach you about the bill.

steps.title: Tick the consent box and send
steps.body: The 'Publish my name' checkbox is required — it is your clear yes. Submit the form, then save the receipt code.

tips: Signing lands dark first. Your name publishes only after a steward reads it in — then it gets an S-number in the public book.
The consent checkbox is what makes signing possible at all. No tick, no signature — the form will not send.
Name, org or town, and your line for the record are the only things that can appear. Email is never published.
guides.source: verified against the live bill platform (semptify.org/bill) on 2026-11-22; drafted per handoffs/library-guide-outline.md

guides.title: Check on something you sent
guides.summary: How to use a receipt code to see where your mark, request, or signature stands on the bill platform at semptify.org/bill. The receipt code is the only way back — nothing public ties a submission to you.

steps.title: Find your receipt code
steps.body: Every time you submit a mark, request, or signature, the page shows a receipt code — a short string of letters and numbers — and tells you to save it. Look where you wrote it down.

steps.title: Open the track page
steps.body: Go to semptify.org/bill and open Track a submission.

steps.title: Enter the code
steps.body: Type or paste the code into the Receipt code box and submit.

steps.title: Read the status
steps.body: The page shows where your submission stands. A mark shows queued or read in — once read in, it shows its M-number and a link to the margin. A signature shows queued or published with its S-number. A request shows its stage: new, reviewing, scheduled, incorporated, or declined.

tips: The receipt code is the only lookup. If you lose it, there is no way to find your submission — save it every time.
Your code is private to you. It never shows on the public pages, and the public pages never show who sent what.
Nothing appearing for a while is normal — a steward reads things in by hand. Check again later with the same code.
